name: Modal serverless GPU containers (per-second, autoscale to zero)
region: multi-region with a regional price multiplier (see notes)
price_basis: per GPU-hour, converted from the page's per-second figures: H100 SXM5 $0.001097/sec = $3.95/hr; H200 SXM $0.001261 = $4.54; B200 $0.001736 = $6.25; B300 $0.001972 = $7.10; A100 80GB $0.000694 = $2.50; A100 40GB $0.000583 = $2.10; L40S $0.000542 = $1.95; A10 $0.000306 = $1.10; L4 $0.000222 = $0.80; T4 $0.000164 = $0.59. Egress $0.04/GiB with 1 TiB/mo free (Starter) or 10 TiB (Team). Fetched 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
$3.95/H100-hour makes Modal the second-cheapest H100 in this slice after Runpod's PCIe, and $0.80 for L4 is the cheapest L4 published anywhere here (vs $0.85 on GCP g2 and $1.67 on AWS g6). But two modifiers on the plan table matter more than the base rate and are easy to miss: 'Region selection 1.15 - 1.75x base prices' and, more importantly, 'Non-preemptible execution 3x base prices'. If you need a container that will NOT be preempted - which for a serving endpoint you probably do - your real H100 rate is $11.85/hr, the most expensive in the slice, not $3.95. Read that row before quoting. Also note Modal bills CPU and memory separately and continuously (a physical core = 2 vCPU, $0.0000131/core/sec; memory $0.00000222/GiB/sec), so a GPU-only comparison understates the all-in cost relative to a hyperscaler VM where vCPU and RAM are bundled into the instance price. On that integrated basis Modal's H100 is not cheaper than AWS p5. What you are buying is scale-to-zero: containers spin up in 1-2 seconds with no minimum billing period and a 60-second default keepalive, versus 10+ minutes to provision a hyperscaler VM where the idle time is billable. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT, stated by Modal itself: AWS, GCP and Azure cloud credits are NOT applicable to Modal usage. Modal transacts through the AWS and GCP marketplaces for committed spend, and offers $30/mo free on Starter and $100/mo on Team, plus up to $10k for academics.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
